claims.text: The initial material is an equiatomic, hot-rolled CrCoNi-based alloy with a primarily FCC structure and limited preexisting short-range order.
Heat treatment can change short-range order in the CoCrNi alloy system.
A targeted short- or medium-time anneal can induce an optimal level of SRO in CrCoNi-based alloys.
The proposed annealing treatment will induce nanoscale compositional clustering.
Suitable temperature-time parameters can induce beneficial SRO while avoiding excessive grain growth and phase segregation.
An inert or controlled annealing atmosphere will prevent oxidation.
The beneficial treatment must preserve a single FCC phase and minimize microstructural coarsening.
Enhanced SRO creates nanoscale precipitates or clusters that act as effective dislocation-pinning sites without hindering plasticity.
Induced SRO changes the local atomic bonding environment.
The SRO-modified bonding environment reduces barriers for dislocation nucleation.
The annealing-induced microstructure promotes dynamic strain hardening.
The proposed mechanism increases load resistance and thereby raises both yield strength and Young's modulus.
The proposed mechanism provides additional controlled-plasticity mechanisms that improve ductility and fracture resistance.
Relative to the as-rolled control, optimized annealing will simultaneously produce statistically significant increases in yield strength, Young's modulus, uniform elongation, and fracture toughness.
Conventional hot-rolled CrCoNi-based alloys have a yield strength of approximately 350 MPa.
Insufficient atomic-level ordering causes conventional hot-rolled CrCoNi-based alloys to have limited stiffness and fracture resistance.
The enhancement may not apply to non-FCC high-entropy-alloy systems or alloys with inadequate elemental mixing.
Atom probe tomography can provide species-specific measurements of SRO and monitor heat-treatment-induced SRO changes in CoCrNi.

Failure of the optimized annealed samples to improve all four targeted properties beyond measurement uncertainty relative to an as-rolled control would refute the stated simultaneous-improvement hypothesis.
